analysis.one_liner: Lets judges re-decide what federal laws mean instead of deferring to the agency that enforces them.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 240-171 in July 2016 with almost no Democratic support; the Senate never voted, and the bill died in committee when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a federal agency enforces a law — on clean air, workplace safety, consumer protection — courts have traditionally deferred to the agency's reading of what the law means. This bill would have changed that: a judge could ignore the agency's interpretation and decide for themselves what the statute and the agency's own rules mean. Businesses that lose agency decisions could more easily persuade a court to overturn the rules. The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote, but the Senate never took it up, and it died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and regulated industries, and their lawyers, gain the most: after an agency issues or applies a rule, they could ask a judge to adopt a different reading of the law, and the judge would have to decide fresh rather than accept the agency's interpretation. More agency decisions become reversible, which raises the cost for agencies to regulate and lowers the cost for regulated parties to challenge rules. Conservatives who believe courts should not defer to executive agencies also get the constitutional outcome they sought.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the federal Administrative Procedure Act so that courts reviewing agency actions must decide 'de novo' — fresh, with no deference — every question of law, including how to interpret statutes and the agencies' own rules
Applies to any action for judicial review of agency action under any law, and no other statute can exempt a case from it except by specifically referring to this section

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the cost would fall mainly on federal regulatory agencies and on the people their rules protect — workers, consumers, patients, and communities — because rules on safety, pollution, wages, and finance would become easier for courts to throw out. It would also make enforcement slower and more expensive, as more cases become contested legal fights over meaning.
analysis.who_pays_short: Agencies and people relying on federal rules

drawbacks.text: Removing judicial deference to agency expertise would make it harder for agencies to protect workers, consumers, and the environment, because regulated industries could relitigate the legal basis of rules in court with judges substituting their own reading for the agency's
The bill applied automatically to every future judicial review of agency action and barred other laws from opting out, a broad rewrite rather than a narrow fix
The House processed it under a rule allowing only one hour of debate and rejected the minority's motion to recommit, so opponents got limited input

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The honest case for the bill was constitutional: unelected agencies have grown enormously powerful, and courts simply deferring to agency interpretations lets the executive branch in effect write its own law. But the practical cost fell on the regulatory system that protects working people — air and water rules, workplace safety standards, financial rules — each of which would become far more vulnerable to being picked apart in court by well-funded industry lawyers, since judges with no technical expertise would substitute their judgment for the agencies'. The bill offered a clean constitutional principle with a heavily one-sided practical beneficiary: businesses seeking to undo regulations. As passed it never became law, so its costs were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in July 2016, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never acted on it, so it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill on July 12, 2016, 240-171, with 239 Republicans in favor and only 1 Democrat
Hours earlier the House rejected, 169-236, a motion to recommit the bill with instructions to add a section excepting rules on preventing firearm transfers to criminals and suspected terrorists
The Senate received the bill on July 13, 2016, read it twice, and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which took no further action
Congress ended January 3, 2017 without the Senate ever voting on the bill, so it died

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Regulated businesses and industries kept the existing standard of judicial deference to agencies, which makes federal protections cheaper to enforce and harder to pick apart in court. Ordinary people's existing regulatory protections were left intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the rules they enforce

for.name: House Judiciary Committee Republicans
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill amended out of committee, 12-8

against.name: 171 of 187 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against final passage, nearly unanimously

against.name: Obama administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as a threat to the executive branch's ability to implement laws, part of its broader objection to Republican regulatory-review legislation in 2016

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Democratic minority included)
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after the Senate received it, leaving it to die

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split sharply by party: 239 of 246 Republicans voted yes and 171 of 187 Democrats voted no, with one Democrat in favor.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (business and trade groups facing federal rules)
industries.note: The bill made every federal rule legally easier to challenge in court, since judges would no longer defer to the agency's reading of the law. Business and conservative legal groups backed it for that reason.
Agencies would lose the interpretive authority that lets them enforce laws Congress wrote broadly — worker safety, environmental, consumer, and financial rules would be more fragile.
